issues.description: coerceNumber silently substitutes 0 for null/undefined, complecting two different facts
issues.detail: The original code used `identity` as ground and `toNumber` as lift; toNumber can return null, and that null would propagate as NaN through arithmetic, which is at least a visible failure mode. The new `coerceNumber: x => toNumber(x) ?? 0` quietly turns 'this value is not a number' into 'this value is zero'. Those are two different facts about the world being complected into one return value. If a non-numeric domain endpoint is a real possibility, the value semantics should be made explicit (reject at the edge, or return NaN, or require pre-cleaned numeric input) rather than buried in an internal adapter.

issues.description: Domain type is declared `number[]` but the function only makes sense for NonEmptyArray<number>
issues.detail: The functions accept `domain: number[]` and then perform a runtime `isNonEmpty` check that throws. The type system already has a name for the precondition (NonEmptyArray<T> is defined at the top of the file), and `peek` now has an overload that returns T for exactly that shape. Accepting `number[]` and then throwing at runtime is the easy choice; the simple choice is to make the parameter `NonEmptyArray<number>` (or `readonly [number, ...number[]]`) and push the emptiness check to the boundary where untrusted input enters. The current shape complects 'I accept any array' with 'but I will reject most of them'.

issues.description: Return type `Domain = [number, number]` hides that the result can legitimately be [NaN, NaN] or [Infinity, ...]
issues.detail: panLog/zoomLog/panPow/zoomPow compose log and pow with arbitrary numeric input; log of a non-positive number is NaN, pow of negative bases with fractional exponents is NaN. The Domain alias asserts 'a pair of numbers' but the value model is really 'a pair of possibly-degenerate numbers'. The new types make the call sites feel safe without making the values safe. Either narrow the input precondition (positive domain for log, etc.) or widen the return type to reflect what actually flows through.

issues.description: Local `identity` shadows and replaces the shared `identity` from accessors.js
issues.detail: The original imported `identity` from `./accessors.js`; the rewrite defines a local `identity: TransformFn = x => x`. That is a small piece of incidental duplication driven by the type signature, not by the problem. If the shared identity needs a narrower type at this call site, give it one once; don't fork a parallel definition that future readers will have to reconcile.

issues.description: New runtime throw on empty domain is a behavior change advertised as a type-safety refactor
issues.detail: The PR description says 'Everything else should have same runtime behavior as before, I just added types' and then in the same breath adds a runtime error for empty domains. That is a real semantic change to the value contract of these functions. It is probably the right change, but it should be called out as a behavior change, not folded into a typing PR — downstream callers that previously got `[NaN, NaN]` back will now get an exception.

issues.description: Two empty-domain tests cover panLinear and zoomLinear but not the other six exported variants
issues.detail: The throw lives inside the shared `pan` and `zoom` helpers, so in practice one test per helper is enough to prove the path. That's fine, but it should be stated — right now the tests imply 'we checked the linear ones' rather than 'we checked the shared helper'. A one-line comment, or a test named after the helper, would make the value of the test match the value of the code.

review.summary: This is a careful, narrow typing pass over a small set of pure functions, and most of the diff is genuinely SIMPLE — values in, values out, no new state, no new identity, no time semantics introduced. The main complecting is in the coerceNumber adapter, which silently fuses "not a number" with "zero" to satisfy a TransformFn signature; that's INCIDENTAL-COMPLEXITY introduced by the types, not by the problem. The Domain input is declared as `number[]` and then guarded at runtime, when the NonEmptyArray type defined at the top of the same file would push the check to the boundary and make the precondition part of the value. The added empty-domain throw is a real behavior change wearing a typing-PR hat and should be named as such. The question that should have been asked first: what is a domain, as a value — is it any array of numbers, or is it a non-empty pair of finite numbers, and where does that get enforced once?
